claims.text: The annual reporting requirements in subsections (a) and (b) TERMINATED effective 31 December 2021. The statutory note reads: 'For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328, set out as a note under section 111 of this title.' Subsections (c) through (g) survive, and (e)(1) still cross-references the terminated (a) and (b).

10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1): 'Not later than March 1 of each year, the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the defense committees a report on special access programs.' Subsection (a)(2) requires, for each SAP in the budget, a brief description, major milestones, actual cost for each prior fiscal year, and estimated total cost plus five out-years.

10 U.S.C. 119(b)(1): 'Not later than February 1 of each year, the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the defense committees a report that, with respect to each new special access program, provides--(A) notice of the designation of the program as a special access program; and (B) justification for such designation.' (b)(2) adds current total program cost estimate and 'an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice.'

10 U.S.C. 119(c)(2): a report on a planned classification change or public declassification of a DoD SAP 'shall be submitted not less than 14 days before the date on which the proposed change or public announcement is to occur' -- but (c)(3) lets the Secretary submit it 'at any time before' if 'because of exceptional circumstances' the 14 days cannot be met, with an explanation.

WAIVER / 'WAIVED SAP' MECHANISM. 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1): 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.' (e)(2): 'If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'

The statutory waiver in 119(e)(2) collapses the notified audience from the full defense committees to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the six named defense committee/subcommittee units -- i.e. a maximum of eight members plus the committee chairs' cleared staff, and the delivery is a briefing 'jointly' rather than a written report to the committees. This is the legal definition of a 'waived' SAP.

10 U.S.C. 119(f): 'A special access program may not be initiated until--(1) the defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.' Note that (f) is NOT among the subsections waivable under (e)(1), which reaches only subsections (a), (b), and (c).

10 U.S.C. 119(d): 'Whenever there is a modification or termination of the policy and criteria used for designating a program of the Department of Defense as a special access program, the Secretary of Defense shall promptly notify the defense committees of such modification or termination.' This is the hook that makes each reissuance of DoDD 5205.07 a reportable event.

10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' as the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations, of the Senate; and the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations, of the House.

REPORTING SUNSET. The GPO text of section 119 carries the note: 'Termination of Reporting Requirements -- For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328, set out as a note under section 111 of this title.' The FY2017 NDAA's blanket report-sunset provision thus terminated the statutory annual SAP report and the annual new-SAP notice as of 31 December 2021.

If the sec. 1061 sunset is read as operative, the only surviving mandatory congressional touchpoints in section 119 after 31 Dec 2021 are (c) declassification notice, (d) criteria-change notice, and (f) the 30-day pre-initiation notice -- i.e. the annual census of SAPs that lets Congress detect an unacknowledged program is precisely the piece that lapsed. Reasoning: (e) waives only (a),(b),(c); the sunset note names only (a) and (b). Whether DoD continued the report voluntarily is not established by any record located here.

desc: Section 119 of title 10 is the only statute that tells the Secretary of Defense what he must tell Congress about special access programs, and it is therefore the exact place to look for how a program escapes oversight. It was added by section 1132(a)(1) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Years 1988 and 1989, Public Law 100-180, signed 4 December 1987, and amended five times since (Pub. L. 101-510 in 1990, Pub. L. 104-106 in 1996, Pub. L. 106-65 in 1999, Pub. L. 107-107 in 2001). The architecture is four affirmative duties and one hole. Subsection (a)(1) requires the Secretary, 'not later than March 1 of each year', to submit to the defense committees 'a report on special access programs' setting forth the total amount requested for DoD SAPs in the President's budget and, for each program, a brief description, major milestones, actual cost for each prior fiscal year, and estimated cost for the current year, the budget year and the four succeeding years. Subsection (b)(1) requires, 'not later than February 1 of each year', notice of the designation of each 'new special access program' and 'justification for such designation', with the current total program cost estimate and 'an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program'. Subsection (c) requires a report at least 14 days before any planned change in the classification of a SAP or any declassification and public release, with an exceptional-circumstances escape hatch. Subsection (d) requires prompt notice of any modification or termination of the policy and criteria used to designate programs as SAPs. Subsection (f) provides that 'A special access program may not be initiated until - (1) the defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.' Subsection (g) defines 'defense committees' as the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees of both chambers plus the defense subcommittees of both Appropriations Committees. Then subsection (e) removes all of it. Nothing in section 119 defines 'special access program', creates a penalty for non-reporting, or gives any committee an enforcement remedy. The duty runs to the Secretary of Defense personally, which means a program concealed from the Secretary of Defense - which is what David Grusch and others allege - produces no statutory violation at all by anyone the statute names.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1) requires that 'not later than March 1 of each year, the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the defense committees a report on special access programs.'

10 U.S.C. 119(a)(2)(B) requires that for each special access program in the budget the report include a brief description, a brief discussion of major milestones, the actual cost for each prior fiscal year of the program, and the estimated total cost plus estimates for the current fiscal year, the budget year, and each of the four succeeding fiscal years.

10 U.S.C. 119(b) requires an annual report, not later than February 1, on each new special access program providing notice of the designation, justification for it, the current estimate of total program cost, and 'an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice.'

10 U.S.C. 119(c) requires the Secretary of Defense to report to the defense committees any planned change in the classification of a DoD special access program, or any planned declassification and public announcement, not less than 14 days beforehand, with a later-notice exception for 'exceptional circumstances' that must be explained in the report.

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive any requirement under subsections (a), (b) or (c) that certain information be included in a report 'if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security,' with any such waiver made on a case-by-case basis.

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) provides that when a waiver is exercised, the withheld information and the justification for the waiver go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' — twelve members in total.

10 U.S.C. 119(f) provides that 'a special access program may not be initiated until— (1) the defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.' The waiver authority in subsection (e) does not extend to subsection (f).

10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' as the Committee on Armed Services, the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations of the Senate, and the corresponding committees and Subcommittee on Defense of the House.

The section was added by Public Law 100-180, division A, title XI, section 1132(a)(1), 4 December 1987, 101 Stat. 1151, and amended by Pub. L. 101-510 (1990), Pub. L. 104-106 (1996), Pub. L. 106-65 (1999) and Pub. L. 107-107 (2001).
Subsection (f), the 30-day pre-initiation notification bar, was added by Pub. L. 101-510, division A, title XIV, section 1482(a)(2), 5 November 1990, and took effect on 1 October 1991.

The statute carries a note headed 'Termination of Reporting Requirements' stating: 'For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328.' The annual SAP report and the annual new-SAP report requirements therefore lapsed at the end of 2021.

DoD Directive 5205.07, effective 12 September 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks, establishes the Special Access Program Oversight Committee chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense and provides that the Director, DoD SAPCO reports directly to the Deputy Secretary and serves as the 'DoD primary point of contact for SAP matters with agencies of the Executive Branch, the Judicial Branch, and the Legislative Branch, including support to SAP congressional meetings, hearings, and responses to congressional inquiries.'

DoD Directive 5205.07 paragraph 3.1(g) provides that 'no DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.'

DoD Directive 5205.07 paragraph 3.1(d) provides that 'establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments will be by exception' and that establishing SAPs to protect new and novel critical program information at any tier 'requires Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense approval.'

Michael Shellenberger testified on 13 November 2024 that a source told him an alleged UAP Unacknowledged Special Access Program 'is controlled by the White House and executed and administrated by the DOD to avoid compliance with Title 10 of the United States Code,' adding 'the White House directed the SECDEF to run it. But that's the loophole.'

Tim Gallaudet testified on 13 November 2024 that 'even the most sensitive Special Access Programs must be reported the Gang of Eight, and all compartmented programs must be reported to the Senate Intelligence Committee,' and that any past failures by DoD and IC components to report UAP programs 'are not only illegal but would have undermined Congress.'

connections: Section 119(f)'s unwaivable 30-day pre-initiation notice is the specific legal provision the alleged White-House-directed, DoD-executed USAP structure is said to be engineered around.
Section 119(e)'s twelve-member disclosure floor is the statutory origin of the waived-SAP practice implemented through DoDD 5205.07, and is what Gallaudet means by 'Gang of Eight' reporting.

The 31 December 2021 termination of subsections (a) and (b) reporting, enacted by section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328 (FY2017 NDAA), coincides with the UAPTF-to-AARO transition and the enactment of 50 U.S.C. 3373 in December 2022.

DoDD 5205.07 places SAP governance under Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks as SAPOC chair and routes all congressional SAP contact through the DoD SAPCO Director, giving a single named office control over what Congress learns.

The contractor gag in DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 3.1(g) directly implicates the defence-contractor layer this board is mapping: contractors cannot lawfully brief Congress on SAP material without DoD SAPCO approval, which structurally converts contractor whistleblowing into a security violation.

USD(I&S) is both the ODNI/IC interface under DoDD 5205.07 and the parent organisation of AARO, meaning the office Congress created to find unreported UAP programs sits inside the office that brokers compartmented sharing between the IC and DoD SAPs.

Luis Elizondo's testimony that he 'managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council' describes the same White-House-to-DoD execution pattern the Immaculate Constellation source alleges, from the inside.
dossier.denialPosture: There is no denial attached to the statute itself. The relevant absence is that no DoD component has ever publicly identified a UAP-related special access program in any section 119 report, and the annual reporting obligations that would have carried such an identification lapsed on 31 December 2021. The Department's only categorical statement in this area is Sue Gough's denial that any SAP named IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION appears in its records.
dossier.narrative:
Section 119 was Congress's answer to the black-budget expansion of the 1980s. Enacted in the FY1988 defense authorisation, it imposed a reporting discipline on a category of program that by design resists reporting. Read as a whole, the section is a fairly aggressive assertion of legislative prerogative, and its subsequent amendment history shows Congress tightening it further: in 1990 Congress added subsection (f), the thirty-day pre-initiation notification bar, effective 1 October 1991, and rewrote subsection (c) to require fourteen days' advance notice of classification changes rather than thirty days' notice after the fact.

The reporting architecture has four parts. Under subsection (a), by 1 March each year the Secretary of Defense must submit to the defense committees a report on special access programs setting out the total amount requested for SAPs in the President's budget and, for each SAP in that budget, a brief description, a brief discussion of major milestones, the actual cost for every prior fiscal year of the program, and the estimated total cost plus estimates for the current year, the budget year, and each of the four succeeding years. Under subsection (b), by 1 February each year the Secretary must report every new SAP with notice of the designation, justification for it, the current estimate of total program cost, and — a provision with real analytic teeth — 'an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice.' That clause exists to stop the Department from hiding duplicate or successor programs under new names. Under subsection (c), any planned classification change or public declassification announcement requires a report to the defense committees not less than fourteen days beforehand, unless exceptional circumstances make that impossible.

Subsection (e) is the pressure valve. The Secretary 'may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report' if inclusion 'would adversely affect the national security,' with the waiver made on a case-by-case basis. When a waiver is used, the withheld information and the justification go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' — that is, to twelve members across six bodies, and to nobody else. This is the statutory basis of what practitioners call a waived SAP. The implementing directive confirms the practice: access to waived SAPs is limited to the chairs, ranking minority members and staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees unless the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves otherwise.

Subsection (f) is the hardest edge in the statute and the one most relevant to this board: 'A special access program may not be initiated until— (1) the defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.' There is no waiver of subsection (f) in subsection (e) — the waiver reaches only (a), (b) and (c). Congress can, in principle, be denied the content of a report about a SAP. It cannot lawfully be denied notice that a DoD SAP is being initiated.

Which makes the terminating note in the current code text the most consequential single fact in this dossier. Under the heading 'Termination of Reporting Requirements,' the statute records: 'For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328.' The annual comprehensive SAP report and the annual new-SAP report both lapsed at the end of 2021, under a sunset written into the FY2017 NDAA. The pre-initiation notification in (f) survives. The routine, systematic, year-over-year visibility does not. Any analyst working this board should note the coincidence of timing: the UAP Task Force was established in August 2020, the ODNI preliminary assessment landed in June 2021, AARO was legislated in December 2021 and stood up in 2022, and the statutory obligation to give Congress an annual accounting of every DoD special access program expired on 31 December 2021.

The implementing machinery underneath the statute is set out in DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued effective 12 September 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks. It establishes the Special Access Program Oversight Committee chaired by the Deputy Secretary, a Senior Review Group, a Senior Working Group, and the DoD Special Access Program Central Office whose Director reports directly to the Deputy Secretary and is the 'DoD primary point of contact for SAP matters with agencies of the Executive Branch, the Judicial Branch, and the Legislative Branch.' Two provisions in it bear directly on the concealment argument. First, establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments is 'by exception' and requires Secretary or Deputy Secretary approval. Second, and more starkly: 'No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.' The contractor layer — precisely where a legacy program would sit — is prohibited by directive from talking to Congress about SAP material without permission from an office reporting to the Deputy Secretary of Defense. And the same directive designates USD(I&S), the office housing AARO, as the primary interface with ODNI for sharing compartmented capabilities into and out of DoD SAPs.

Witnesses have made the statutory argument directly. Tim Gallaudet told House Oversight in November 2024 that 'even the most sensitive Special Access Programs must be reported the Gang of Eight' and that 'any and all past failures by DoD and IC components to report UAP programs and activities are not only illegal but would have undermined Congress by preventing it from exercising its legislative and oversight responsibilities.' Shellenberger's source described the alleged workaround with unusual precision: the White House directs the Secretary of Defense to run the program, so it is executed by DoD but controlled by the White House. 'But that's the loophole.' Whether such a structure escapes subsection (f) turns on whether it is a special access program 'of the Department of Defense' — a question no court and no committee has resolved on the public record.
openQuestions: Has the section 119(e) waiver authority ever been exercised for a UAP-related program, and do the twelve recipients' offices hold the resulting notifications?

Was the 31 December 2021 termination of the subsection (a) and (b) annual reports replaced by any successor reporting vehicle, or is there now no periodic comprehensive SAP accounting to Congress at all?

Is a program directed by the White House and executed by the Secretary of Defense a 'special access program of the Department of Defense' for purposes of subsection (f)? No court or committee has resolved this on the public record.
Who is the current Director of the DoD Special Access Program Central Office, and what records does that office hold of SAP material provided to Congress?

Does any section 119 report ever filed identify a program with a UAP, materials-exploitation or recovered-technology mission, and would the subsection (b)(2)(B) similar-technology identification requirement have forced such a disclosure?
How does section 119 interact with intelligence-community programs funded outside the DoD budget, where the reporting path runs to the intelligence committees rather than the defense committees?
dossier.whatItIs: 10 U.S.C. § 119, 'Special access programs: congressional oversight,' is the statute that governs how the Department of Defense must tell Congress about its special access programs. Enacted 4 December 1987 as section 1132(a)(1) of Public Law 100-180 and amended in 1990, 1996, 1999 and 2001, it requires an annual report on all SAPs, an annual report on each new SAP with justification, advance notice of classification changes, and — decisively — bars any SAP from being initiated until the defense committees have been notified and thirty days have elapsed. It also grants the Secretary of Defense a case-by-case waiver over the content of those reports.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the statute against which the concealment must be measured, and it is the statute a whistleblower report given to Congress in 2024 alleges is being deliberately circumvented. Subsection (f) is categorical: a special access program 'may not be initiated until' the defense committees are notified and thirty days pass. If a legacy retrieval or reverse-engineering effort exists as a DoD SAP and the defense committees were never notified, the illegality is not a matter of interpretation. Subsection (e) is the built-in escape hatch, letting the Secretary strip content from the reports on national-security grounds and narrow disclosure to twelve members. And the reporting obligations in subsections (a) and (b) were terminated outright effective 31 December 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328 — the annual SAP report to Congress simply stopped, in the same window in which the UAP Task Force was being stood up and AARO was being legislated. Michael Shellenberger's sworn testimony that an alleged UAP USAP is White-House-controlled and DoD-executed 'to avoid compliance with Title 10' is a claim about this section specifically.

timeline.label: Congress first requires DoD to report special access programs
timeline.text: President Reagan signs Public Law 100-180. Section 1132(a)(1) adds section 119 to title 10, creating for the first time a statutory duty to tell the defense committees that a special access program exists. Every alleged legacy activity from the 1940s to this date ran under no SAP reporting obligation at all. The same section creates the subsection (e) waiver in the same breath.
